💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that who understands the struggles and successes of a designer better than another designer?
  • According to recent reports, “When we introduced ROOM’s Designers on Design series, the idea was simple: create a space for designers to have the kinds of conversations that don’t always happen in the day-to-day,” indicates Elyse Heckman, SVP, Brand & Communications at ROOM.
  • According to recent reports, hospitality legend Anda Andrei of Anda Andrei Design and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich of Goodrich design studio sit down for a discussion in the most recent installation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that who understands the struggles and successes of a designer better than another designer? That’s the core concept behind ROOM’s Designers on Design video series, which pairs leading designers together for open conversation on the future of architecture, design, and human connection.

According to recent reports, “When we introduced ROOM’s Designers on Design series, the idea was simple: create a space for designers to have the kinds of conversations that don’t always happen in the day-to-day,” indicates Elyse Heckman, SVP, Brand & Communications at ROOM. “No interviewer, no moderator, no prescribed talking points. Just two creative minds coming together to exchange ideas, challenge perspectives, and explore what moves the industry forward.”.

According to recent reports, hospitality legend Anda Andrei of Anda Andrei Design and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich of Goodrich design studio sit down for a discussion in the most recent installation. Unlike earlier episodes of this series, Andrei and Goodrich know each other outside of the studio—and have for years. Goodrich attributes his love of hospitality design to Andrei’s hotels, while Andrei has had a front-row seat to the evolution of Goodrich’s career. (Plus, their work shares a certain symbiosis: Andrei’s recent renovation of the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris aligns with Goodrich’s past in museum exhibition design.).

“For this episode, we wanted to take a slightly different approach to our previous pairings,” says Heckman. “Rather than bringing together designers who may be meeting for the first time, we were drawn to the idea of connecting two individuals who already share a history and familiarity with each other’s work. We loved the opportunity to explore how those relationships shape our perspectives, influence our creative instincts and ultimately help us grow as designers.”.

Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM.

Industry observers note that tapping into the spirit of authentic exchange that ROOM set out to foster, the duo’s conversation begins with their first (almost) meeting. In 2003, Goodrich was helping his partner, Barnes Foundation Executive Director Thomas Collins, open Zaha Hadid’s Contemporary Arts Center in Cincinnati when he heard that Andrei would be there in 20 minutes. “I looked to Thom, and I remarked, ‘You’ve got to go home, take a shower, and put on a suit. This is a massive deal,’” Goodrich shares.

However, the pair didn’t officially meet until years later—after Andrei had left the Ian Schrager Company, starting her own firm at 59 years old. “You came very highly recommended, and I wanted to hire you,” she says. “But then I asked you a crucial question: ‘Have you ever opened a hotel before?’” “And I had to say no,” Goodrich adds.

Designing a hotel is no easy feat, which Goodrich learned when opening his first hotel, Arlo SoHo, in 2016. He shared how the final month before opening was chaos. With nearly 40 years shaping hospitality projects, Andrei knows this reality well—but emphasizes that it’s even more painful when operations start changing after the design is finished. Like living organisms, hospitality projects evolve with the staff, users, and guests over the years.

Industry observers note that still, the pair agree that all these concerns and pain points provide valuable lessons. “Understanding how operations affect the success of restaurants and of hotels is foundational for making great designs,” Goodrich says.

Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM.

On the topic of design inspiration, Andrei believe the best hotels have a story. Much like an elevator pitch, she believes projects should have a one-sentence design concept. For example, at the Delano Miami Beach Hotel, which she created in collaboration with Philippe Starck, the one-liner was: “a Greek fisherman that finds a diamond in the sea.” Goodrich agrees with the sentiment of this design tool: “If you have that short phrase, if you can go back to the essence of what your concept is, things fall into place.”.

Throughout the episode, there is a sense of mutual respect and deep appreciation for the other’s work. Goodrich calls Andrei a superhero collaborator, while Andrei compliments Goodrich’s work (and name). Both value collaboration, imagination, and challenging work. Heckman sees the pair’s connection as proof of the series’ larger purpose: “It’s a wonderful example of how seemingly different creative paths can intersect, and how the work we encounter early in our careers can continue to influence us in unexpected ways.”.

“When you started your company, we had some empty desks in my office and we shared offices. And who knew that nine and a half years later, we would be sitting here and talking about how amazing you did,” Andrei indicates with a laugh.

This is what ROOM’s Designers on Design series does so well: It brings design to the human level. From the ideas and experiences that shape the work to the friends, colleagues, and mentors who leave a lasting impact, each episode looks at the people behind the portfolio.

Industry observers note that “What makes this episode especially compelling is that the conversation extends beyond design itself,” shares Heckman. “It gets to the heart of how we become the designers we are — the people who influence us, the experiences that shape our creative instincts, and the ways inspiration gets passed from one generation to the next. In that sense, it embodies exactly what we hoped the series would become: a platform for authentic exchange, unexpected perspectives and the stories behind the work.”.

Industry observers note that and who knows? The series might even inspire new work of its own. “I want to do a project together,” Andrei says. Goodrich answers: “I know, me too. That’s my dream.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a new place in residential design.
  • According to recent reports, the interest goes beyond athletic recovery.
  • In the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a new place in residential design. As the wellness practice grows in popularity, homeowners are increasingly looking to incorporate cold therapy directly into their bathrooms, transforming what was once a standalone piece of fitness equipment into an integrated feature of the home.

According to recent reports, the interest goes beyond athletic recovery. Cold-water immersion has been associated with potential benefits ranging from reduced muscle soreness to improved sleep and stress management, although research into its broader health effects remains limited. Still, the appeal is evident. According to Houzz’s 2024 Summer Trends Report, searches for “cold plunge” increased 74% year over year, while searches for “indoor sauna” rose 69%.

In the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging. Photography by Steve C. Wilson.

That interest reflects a larger shift toward wellness-focused residential spaces. The manufacturer’s 2026 report found that searches for “wellness room” had increased 164%, suggesting that homeowners are thinking more intentionally about how their environments can support relaxation and well-being.

For interior designers, these changing priorities are introducing upcoming considerations into residential projects. Arizona-based designer Stephanie Larsen, who incorporates cold plunges, infrared saunas, and integrated aromatherapy systems into her work, has seen clients place greater emphasis on these features. “Today’s clients are craving homes that heal and inspire,” she told Luxe Interiors + Design. “They want spaces infused with wellness technology.”.

Accommodating those requests means thinking beyond individual fixtures to how different wellness experiences function together. Cold plunges, for instance, are often paired with saunas for contrast therapy, which alternates between hot and cold exposure. Bringing both into a residential setting requires careful consideration of available space, plumbing, and the relationship between the different elements. Manufacturers, meanwhile, are developing more integrated systems that offer greater flexibility.

Hydro Systems integrates cold-plunge technology into freestanding bathtubs, bringing cold therapy into residential bathrooms without the need for separate equipment. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

“We’re seeing wellness become a more intentional part of residential design, with dedicated spaces that bring together multiple hydrotherapy experiences in a single tub, from cold plunging and whirlpool to oxygenated microbubble therapy,” says Ashley Steinhardt, VP of Sales at Hydro Systems.

According to recent reports, the California-based bath manufacturer has developed its Hydro Chill technology to incorporate cold plunging into customizable bathtubs, eliminating the need for a separate fixture. Its latest iteration also introduces smart-home functionality, allowing users to adjust water temperatures and schedule plunges remotely.

Hydro Systems is also exploring how multiple hydrotherapy experiences can share the same footprint. Its upcoming Hydro Chill Ultra delivers both hot and cold water through a self-contained system that generates its own hot water. Because it doesn’t require a traditional hot-water connection, the technology offers additional flexibility for installations in pool houses and dedicated wellness rooms.

Industry observers note that featured in an Atlanta Homes Showhouse, Hydro Systems’ Slate bathtub features a custom color and polished finish, with integrated Hydro Chill cold-plunge technology. Paired with a wood-paneled sauna, the tub demonstrates how cold therapy can become part of a thoughtfully designed residential wellness space. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

Industry observers note that while expansive home spas provide room for separate saunas, plunge tubs, and other amenities, integrating hydrotherapy into an existing bathroom requires a different approach. Multifunctional fixtures can help reduce the space needed for these experiences, making them easier to accommodate within conventional residential layouts.

Industry observers note that “Wellness doesn’t have to be confined to a dedicated room,” Steinhardt says. “Hydrotherapy can also be incorporated into smaller bathroom footprints, bringing wellness into everyday routines.”.

Hydro Systems’ Hydro Chill cold-plunge system is incorporated into a home gym alongside weight-training equipment, bringing cold-water immersion into a dedicated fitness and recovery space. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

Cold plunges may still be a relatively niche residential amenity, but their growing visibility is prompting designers to reconsider what a bathroom can accommodate. As more wellness features make their way into the home, the challenge will be integrating them without compromising the functionality, comfort, and aesthetics of the spaces around them.

It has been revealed that there’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness.

In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance consumers are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

According to recent reports, on the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

Preview both fields: username indicates text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

In a recent development, add a fresh scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

In a recent development, preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

According to recent reports, at the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:.

According to recent reports, enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:.

Sources indicate that find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

It has been revealed that wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:.

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:.

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do consumers understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

Industry observers note that this is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Art Basel will compensate dealers for the early closure of its Paris fair, held from 20-23 October in the Grand Palais, the fair company announced today (11th November), on a French national holiday.

Sources indicate that the fair was forced to shut down its Parisian outing two days early because of violent rioting in the French capital. Since then, dealers have been demanding compensation for their lost sales and stand fees. Indeed, soon after the closure the French Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) sent a strongly worded letter to the fair director, Karim Crippa. It accused the firm of not consulting with dealers—the CPGA represents 57 of the fair’s 211 exhibitors—and of showing “disrespect, even contempt” for them.

The closure hit the smaller dealers particularly hard, since the biggest galleries tended to make sales on the opening days, whereas the smaller dealers, mainly sited on the upper floor of the Grand Palais, depended on the two weekend days for business. The letter mentioned it expected “concrete proposals” for this compensation.

Recent findings suggest that crippa has responded to the letter with an offer of a reduction across the board of 20% of stand fees to all participants. He noted: “We believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further.”.

Philippe Charpentier of Mor Charpentier gallery, who is the president of the CPGA, tells The Art Newspaper that the compensation rate is what the committee expected.

Nonetheless, if one calculates in percentages, the fair was open for three-and-a-half days—its ultra-VIP Avant-Première timeslot began at 3pm on Tuesday 20 October, and the fair closed on Friday—instead of the projected five-and-a-half. The fair was therefore shortened by about 36%.

Industry observers note that speaking about the decision to close the fair early, Noah Horowitz, the chief executive of Art Basel, tells The Art Newspaper: “We stand by the decision to close. We feel it was in the right interest of all the parties involved. It was a very difficult decision, but we stand by it.”.

Asked about the decision to close for the two days—when unrest was only expected on the Saturday—he claims: “Given the uncertainty surrounding the impact and the duration of the planned demonstrations and access to the Grand Palais, we simply couldn't be confident that conditions would allow us to reopen safely on Sunday. An event of this size and scale is incredibly complex, and some exhibitors had also expressed serious concerns about leaving artworks unattended in the Grand Palais on the weekend. We concluded that closing the fair early was in the best interests of the art, the staff and ultimately the visitors.”.

According to recent reports, horowitz is not prepared to comment on other aspects of the closure—for example, questions of insurance or the firm’s relationship with the Grand Palais, for which MCH paid €10.6m to rent the space for seven years in 2022. Horowitz indicates that MCH, the parent manufacturer of the Basel group of art fairs, is "fully committed to delivering the 2027 edition of the fair".

Recent findings suggest that the most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:.

It has been revealed that the "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

In a recent development, these definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

Recent findings suggest that A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

Industry observers note that this explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Sources indicate that income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

Industry observers note that the FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

According to recent reports, what distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Sources indicate that income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

Sources indicate that the distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Industry observers note that add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

In a recent development, according to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Sources indicate that lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • ‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world. The RISD graduate, who earned her BFA in furniture design, already has more than 20 exhibitions under her belt. Now she’s adding curator to her résumé with 260 Madison, an artist-run exhibition bringing together more than 50 artists across a former Duane Reade storefront and a 23,000-square-foot office floor above it in Midtown Manhattan.

It has been revealed that tabak’s own work is equally expansive. Drawing on history, technology, and materiality, she explores the relationship between the digital and physical worlds, often starting with digitally modeled forms that she translates into sculptures through hands-on processes such as cutting, perforation, lamination, and extrusion.

‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

In a recent development, but her interest in materials extends beyond their physical properties. She also sees them as records of labor, manufacturing, extraction, and use. Her work examines contemporary material culture through a historical lens, imagining how the things made and valued today might be understood generations from now. As she puts it, her sculptures are “less concerned with imagining the future than with creating historical distance from the present.”.

Industry observers note that that perspective comes through in her recent work, which examines the increasingly blurred line between looking and shopping. In her Brooklyn studio, the Queens-born artist has been embedding collected industrial objects in three-ply cardboard, referencing the packaging and shipping systems that support consumer culture. She’s also exploring the influence of visual search and algorithmic commerce, where objects spotted in an image can lead to an endless stream of purchasable alternatives. It’s a commentary on a culture in which images don’t just inspire desire; they generate transactions.

‘First Water (deer)’ and ‘First Water (banner)’ (2026) by Dexter Barker-Glenn on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

For today’s Friday Five, we spent five minutes with Shaina Tabak to explore the ideas behind her curatorial debut at 260 Madison and the influences shaping her own work in the exhibition.

‘Ghosts’ (2025) by Alisa Berger and ‘Impaler Shield’ (2026) by Kari Cholnoky on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

It has been revealed that for her curatorial debut, Tabak drew on Columbia University’s MFA community and her own network of artists, bringing together emerging talents and established names. Co-curated by artistic duo Dayana Matasheva and Edson Niebla Rodríguez of Demon Lovers, Inc., 260 Madison includes artists such as Simon Denny, Jon Kessler, and Eva and Franco Mattes. The exhibition was organized in collaboration with the building’s owner, AmTrustRE, which gave the curators full creative control.

‘Longcat’ (2026) by Eva & Franco Mattes on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

According to recent reports, on view through Nov. 22, 2026, the expansive exhibition brings together familiar materials, objects, and technologies that are dismantled, reconstructed, or made strange. Exposed HVAC, ripped-out toilets, and corporate-logo wallpaper create the backdrop for works spanning sculpture, new media, and video. Tabak’s goal for 260 Madison is to “examine the systems organizing contemporary life—from control, surveillance, AI, and extraction to the material and architectural structures that shape how we work, move, and live.”.

Below, in her own words, Tabak shares the influences that shaped her approach to 260 Madison, from artist-run exhibitions that challenged traditional institutions to architectural theories and sculptures that informed her own work.

Shaina Tabak’s works ‘Localized Collapse / Frozen Zone’ (2026) and ‘Sweep Towards Skylight’ (2026) on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of the artist.

“The first one, Damien Hirst’s Freeze (1988), was suggested to me by my professor Jon Kessler. Freeze was particularly compelling because it took place amid the redevelopment of London’s Docklands and was itself supported by real-estate developers, revealing the uneasy relationship between artistic independence and the production of urban capital. That history made me particularly conscious of a contradiction in our own project: While 260 Madison temporarily interrupts the building’s commercial function, the exhibition also generates cultural value for a property undergoing modernization.”.

According to recent reports, “A more recent exhibition, Christopher Wool’s See Stop Run (2024), took place in New York City’s Financial District and demonstrated how artists could operate outside established institutions by appropriating vacant commercial spaces. Wool’s exhibition was also installed on a gutted office floor and offered a more immediate architectural reference, allowing the building’s exposed infrastructure and traces of demolition to enter into dialogue with the work. With 260 Madison, we wanted to push these precedents even further, treating the vacant corporate office as a material record of changing relationships between labor, capital, and the built environment.”.

Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

Industry observers note that “Rem Koolhaas’ book Delirious Latest York and his essay “Junkspace” were really helpful in connecting the architecture of the space to the exhibition. My partner has worked on the 17th floor of 260 Madison for the past three years—a complete coincidence—and his 9-to-5 job as a paralegal brought to mind Koolhaas’ concepts of the vertical schism, architectural lobotomy, and definitive instability as I considered the exhibition’s function.”.

“All three of Koolhaas’ concepts, in their own ways, describe the Manhattan skyscraper as a structure in which the exterior remains independent of the interior, allowing different floors to accommodate radically different and constantly changing activities without altering the building’s outward appearance.”.

“I was thinking about House, a temporary public sculpture by Rachel Whiteread, when creating my sculpture Swept Towards Skylight (2026) for 260 Madison. I embedded an earlier work in insulation foam and coated it with cement to give the illusion that the negative space around it had been cast solid. Whiteread’s work transformed the interior of a house slated for demolition into a concrete monument to its former inhabitants and the lives that had occupied it.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I kept returning to this idea while curating 260 Madison, where the vacant office floor still bears physical traces of the labor and routines that once animated it. I wanted the building to function not simply as a container for artworks, but as an artifact in its own right, with its exposed infrastructure and signs of abandonment becoming part of the exhibition. What interests me about House, and what I hoped to capture at 260 Madison, was how architecture outlives its function and becomes a monument to the systems that once gave it meaning.”.

260 Madison is on view through Nov. 22, 2026, at 260 Madison Avenue in Latest York City.

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The HTTP Archive Web Almanac has been tracking color contrast failures for years. The numbers have barely moved. After half a decade of design system tooling, accessibility linters, and entire JavaScript libraries dedicated to computing readable text colors, 70% of websites still fail basic WCAG contrast checks in 2025. The WebAIM Million paints an even grimmer picture — 83.9% of homepages flagged for low contrast text in 2026, up from 79.1% in 2025. The rate improves by maybe a few percentage points per year on one benchmark and actually gets worse on another. That’s not progress — that’s proof that relying on runtime JavaScript for something this fundamental doesn’t scale across the open web. We didn’t need better libraries. We’ve needed better CSS.

The contrast-color() function is that better CSS. One declaration. The browser runs the contrast math during style computation, before the page paints, and hands you the right text color. No library, no build step, no hydration flash.

Note: If you’ve seen it called color-contrast() in older articles and spec drafts — that name was changed, and the old syntax no longer works in any browser.

Recent findings suggest that the Level 5 version is simple. You give it a color. It gives you back black or white, whichever has more contrast against your input.

Change --brand-color to neon green, text goes black. Change it to midnight navy, text goes white. Swap themes at runtime via JavaScript and the text adapts instantly — no event listeners, no recalculation.

A few things to know about the current version:.

Recent findings suggest that this function lives across two specifications. That’s unusual and worth understanding.

CSS Color Level 5 defines what browsers ship today. One color in, black or white out. The algorithm is deliberately marked “UA-defined”, meaning the browser decides what math to use internally. Right now, every engine uses WCAG 2.x relative luminance. But that “UA-defined” label isn’t accidental — it’s a planned escape hatch.

It has been revealed that you’ll see APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) mentioned a lot in this context. APCA models how human eyes actually perceive contrast, factoring in font weight, spatial frequency, and ambient light — a genuine improvement over the WCAG 2.x formula. By not locking “use WCAG 2.x” into the Level 5 spec, browser vendors could swap to APCA later without breaking any existing code. If the spec had shipped with a wcag2() keyword as the default, every site using it would’ve been stuck on the old math permanently.

Recent findings suggest that but APCA’s future is far less certain than the hype suggests. Adrian Roselli’s “WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026” lays out the current situation clearly: APCA was pulled from the WCAG 3 working draft in mid-2023 after failing to gain enough Working Group support. The WCAG 3 spec currently says the contrast algorithm is “yet to be determined,” and the standard itself may not be finalized until 2030 or later. Roselli also filed a Chromium matter in May 2024 asking for the “Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm” experiment flag to be removed from DevTools entirely, arguing that the implementation is outdated and risks misleading developers into thinking APCA is further along — or more official — than it actually is. That issue is still open.

It has been revealed that none of this means APCA is dead. The research behind it is peer-reviewed and substantive, and its creator has noted that colors passing APCA guidelines greatly exceed WCAG 2 minimums in the vast majority of cases. But right now, there is no guarantee APCA will be the algorithm that replaces WCAG 2.x — and that uncertainty matters for contrast-color(). If a different algorithm wins out, or if WCAG 3 adopts something entirely latest, the “UA-defined” label means browsers can adapt without breaking your code. It also means the Level 6 features — candidate color lists, target ratios, the tbd-fg/tbd-bg keywords — are all designed around an algorithm that may or may not materialize in its current form.

CSS Color Level 6 adds the extended syntax — candidate color lists and target contrast ratios:.

According to recent reports, the browser would evaluate each candidate left to right and pick the first that meets the 4.5:1 AA threshold. The tbd-fg and tbd-bg keywords indicate whether the base color is foreground or background, which matters for directional contrast models like APCA. This is all Working Draft territory — doubly so given APCA’s uncertain status. Use the Level 5 version for now.

This one’s in better shape than most upcoming CSS features. All three major engines have shipped it in stable releases: Chrome 147 (April 2026), Firefox 146, and Safari 26.0. It reached Baseline Newly Available status in April 2026. Check caniuse for the full version matrix. All three engines pass the Web Platform Tests for contrast-color(), which means the edge cases (e.g., tie-breaking logic, color space conversion, syntax parsing) behave the same across browsers.

It has been revealed that the raw global support percentage on caniuse looks low, but that mostly reflects enterprise browsers and people who never patch. If you’re reading this, your browser almost certainly supports it already.

Progressive enhancement is straightforward using @supports:.

Recent findings suggest that older browsers get white text with a dark shadow for legibility. Supporting browsers get the native calculation. Nobody sees broken text.

One thing to watch for: automated accessibility scanners (Lighthouse, Axe, etc.) can’t evaluate text-shadow. They only look at the computed color against background-color. So the fallback will still get flagged as a contrast failure in CI/CD pipelines, even if the shadow makes the text perfectly legible to human eyes. If your team runs automated a11y checks, you may need to allowlist that specific rule or add a comment explaining why the flag is a false positive.

This can trip people up: “I used the contrast function, so my site passes accessibility checks now, right?”.

Recent findings suggest that mathematically? Usually yes. There is a persistent myth that for certain “mid-tone” backgrounds, both black and white fail the standard WCAG 4.5:1 AA ratio. That’s mathematically false. Under the WCAG 2.x relative luminance formula, there is absolutely no background color where both pure black and pure white fail AA. One (or both) will always pass.

In a recent development, take #2277d3 (a medium blue). It sits right on a mathematical knife-edge where both black and white actually pass AA (both hit roughly 4.58:1). contrast-color() will hand you whichever has the slight mathematical edge.

But here is the actual gotcha: the WCAG 2.x math has known perceptual blind spots. That same #2277d3 with black text mathematically passes AA, but to human eyes, it can be incredibly difficult to read. contrast-color() gives you mathematical compliance, which is great for automated audits, but that doesn’t always equal perceptual accessibility. (This is exactly why APCA exists and why the spec was designed to let browsers swap algorithms later.).

Furthermore, if you’re aiming for the stricter WCAG AAA standard (7.0:1), a true dead zone does exist. For backgrounds with a luminance between roughly 10% and 30%, neither black nor white will hit 7:1. In those cases, contrast-color() can’t save you — it just hands you the “least bad” failing option.

If you’re animating a background from white to black on hover:.

Sources indicate that the background fades smoothly over one second. But because the Level 5 output is a discrete value (black or white), the text color can’t be interpolated. It snaps.

And here is the visual gotcha: the snap doesn’t happen halfway through. If you’ve been building themes for a while, you probably have muscle memory from the old Sass days, where we checked if lightness($bg) > 50%. That relied on HSL lightness, where 50% is the geometric midpoint.

But WCAG 2.x relative luminance is a non-linear scale. Under the WCAG formula, the mathematical tipping point — where black and white have identical contrast against the background — actually occurs at approximately 18% relative luminance (specifically ~17.9%).

Recent findings suggest that because of that, the visual behavior during a white-to-black fade is heavily skewed. The text doesn’t snap in the middle. It stays black for the vast majority of the animation, only snapping to white at the very tail-end of the transition when the background gets extremely dark. It’s a jarring, late hard cut.

You might assume transition-behavior: allow-discrete fixes this. It doesn’t. allow-discrete does not fix the jarring visual experience because it cannot interpolate a binary output; it only shifts the timing of the hard snap to the 50% mark of the animation duration. If you need smooth text color transitions, you’ll have to layer color-mix() or manage the crossfade yourself.

Industry observers note that if the background is a perfect middle gray where both black and white produce identical contrast ratios, the spec has a hardcoded tiebreaker: white wins. Not a big deal in practice, but worth knowing if you’re debugging gray palettes and the text isn’t doing what you expect.

In a recent development, the function takes a flat value. You can’t pass it a gradient or a url(). contrast-color(linear-gradient(...)) is a parse error. If your background is a photo or a complex gradient, you still need JavaScript or manually color-pick for overlay text.

Recent findings suggest that pass a semi-transparent color, and the browser blends it against an assumed opaque canvas (usually white) before running the contrast math. It’s not ignoring your alpha channel — it’s compositing it. But the result might surprise you if you expected the function to “see through” to whatever’s actually behind the element.

If a user enables Windows High Contrast, the forced-colors: active media query kicks in and the browser aggressively overwrites author-defined colors. contrast-color() bows out — forced system colors like CanvasText take over completely. You don’t need to write manual media queries to undo your contrast logic; the browser handles the hierarchy.

Black or white sounds limiting, but once you feed that output into other CSS color functions, you can build an entire component palette off a single custom property.

Pure black text on a vibrant card looks fine. Pure white on a coral card can feel flat. What if the contrast text was a very dark or very light tint of the background color instead?

Kevin Hamer explored related territory in his CSS-Tricks piece “Approximating contrast-color() With Other CSS Features”, where he used OKLCH lightness and round() to approximate the black/white switch without contrast-color() — essentially oklch(from round(1.21 - l) 0 0). That’s a polyfill strategy: get the binary light/dark decision working in browsers that don’t support the native function yet. What we’re doing here is different — we start with contrast-color()’s native output and then enrich it by injecting the background’s own hue:.

When contrast-color() returns white, l is 1 (full lightness). When it returns black, l is 0. By pulling the background’s hue back in and adding a touch of chroma, you get text that reads as a deep dark indigo or a pale icy indigo instead of generic black/white. Hamer’s approach gives you the black/white decision without browser support; this one takes the decision the browser already made and gives it personality.

Fair warning: By tweaking the lightness and chroma of the black/white output, you can push a borderline contrast ratio into failing territory. Always run your tinted output through an accessibility linter before shipping.

Also worth noting: This example chains two very modern features — contrast-color() and oklch(from ...). If either one isn’t supported, the entire declaration fails silently. Your @supports block needs to test for both:.

Similar idea, simpler API. Mix the sharp black/white output back into the background to soften it:.

It has been revealed that one custom property driving text, border, and potentially box-shadow or outline. Change --alert-color and the entire component recalculates.

Industry observers note that this pattern also works well for ::placeholder text, which is a common pain point in dynamic theming. Placeholder text should be readable but visually softer than the input’s main text — color-mix() with contrast-color() gets you there:.

50% mix gives you a muted but legible placeholder that adapts automatically to whatever background the input sits on.

For apps that support system light/dark mode:.

Sources indicate that when the operating system switches to dark mode, --surface resolves to #121212, and contrast-color() returns white. No media queries, no JavaScript theme detection. The whole chain resolves natively.

In a recent development, the practical payoff: every one of these libraries existed because CSS couldn’t do contrast math. If you’re only using them for readable-text-color selection, you can pull them out of your runtime entirely:.

You might still need these for generating complex color scales, but the contrast-for-readability use case is now covered natively.

Beyond bundle size, there’s a performance angle that’s easy to overlook. Those JavaScript libraries don’t just cost you network bytes — they run on the main thread. Every time a theme changes or a component mounts with a dynamic background, your JS has to parse the color, compute luminance, decide black or white, and write the result back to the DOM. That’s main-thread work competing with layout, event handlers, and everything else your app is doing. contrast-color() moves all of that into the browser’s native style computation phase — heavily optimized C++ that runs before paint. For apps with lots of themed components, that’s a real difference in responsiveness.

There’s also a subtle bug that goes away: hydration flash. In React or Vue SSR apps, the server renders HTML without JavaScript. The client then hydrates, running JS to calculate contrast and inject the correct text color. For a brief window between initial paint and hydration, the text is either invisible or the wrong color. Moving contrast into CSS eliminates that entirely — the browser resolves the correct color during the initial paint, before JavaScript loads.

For context on what this replaces:.

Sources indicate that sass era. You’d write a function that checked lightness($bg) > 50% and returned black or white at compile time. Worked for static themes. Completely useless for user-picked colors, CMS palettes, or dark mode, because the output was baked into the CSS file and could never change at runtime.

Recent findings suggest that the variable toggle hack. When CSS custom properties shipped, people got creative. GitHub used a version of this for their issue label picker — splitting colors into --r, --g, --b channels, calculating Rec.709 luminance inside calc(), multiplying by negative infinity, and clamping to 0 or 1. It worked. It was also unreadable, unmaintainable, and would break silently if you got one parenthesis wrong. (Kevin Hamer’s OKLCH-based approximation is the most elegant version of this lineage — cleaner math, better perceptual alignment — but it’s still a workaround for a function that now ships natively.).

Recent findings suggest that contrast-color() replaces all of these approaches with a single function call. And because the spec lets browsers upgrade the underlying algorithm, your code won’t need to change if and when a successor to WCAG 2.x contrast math lands — whether that’s APCA or something else entirely.

Recent findings suggest that that 70% failure rate was never about developers refusing to care about contrast. It was about the distance between caring and shipping — the library, the build step, the runtime calculation, the hydration flash, the one component someone forgot to wire up. Every gap in that chain was a spot where accessibility quietly dropped out.

In a recent development, contrast-color() doesn’t make developers care more. It makes caring cost nothing.

Porto Rocha builds the Almeida & Dale brand identity on Diakritik AD, a custom typeface, and one strong blue for Brazil's biggest gallery.

The blue arrives before anything else. Porto Rocha paints the gallery's newly introduced wordmark black on a single strong blue, and that blue becomes the system: cards, catalogues, fair posters, the facade. Almeida & Dale was founded in 1998 and, after its 2025 merger with Millan, became Latin America's largest gallery, with three locations in Brazil and a new SÃ£o Paulo flagship opening in 2026. Yet the work never shouts about scale. It reads as one confident voice, and the artwork leads every layout.

According to recent reports, the type carries the idea. Diakritik AD is a custom face drawn with type designer Marek Nedelka, mid-century condensed proportions tightened into precise contemporary geometry. It was engineered for Brazilian Portuguese, its diacritics drawn at the same weight as the letterforms, so names like JosÃ© Bento hold their accents without apology.

Sources indicate that A second voice keeps it human. Bull-5 borrows the raw, mechanical feel of typewriter print labels from 1980s American newspaper archives, and the two faces trade roles across the system: Diakritik commands at poster scale, Bull-5 adds texture in the small print. Dynamic grids and flexible hierarchy let the same rules build a catalogue spread or a fair booth.

The blue is the break from the category. Most blue-chip galleries hide behind black and white neutrality; Almeida & Dale owns a single color and lets it signal trust. It runs across business cards, the binder, the pencil and the FAIRS 2026 foldout, always flat, always the same blue, never decoration.

At architectural scale the system goes quiet. The facade carries the wordmark small and black on white, the gallery walls carry exhibition titles in huge black type, and inside, the rooms stay white and the art does the talking. Full-bleed catalogue spreads and fair posters give the work range without losing the thread.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular. The choices are a balancing act, forcing carmakers to weigh price, safety, convenience, and appearance to determine which substance makes the most sense for the masses.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

It has been revealed that but what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns? What if cost was no object, practicality a formality, and there was no need to cater to the wants of more than one owner? Well, that was the lucky circumstance designer Fabrizio Giugiaro, founder and CEO of GFG Style, found himself in when creating the Peralta D, a gran turismo with a body made of hand-hammered copper.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

“It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro says. The duo had worked together before on the design house’s first one-off automobile, the spitshine-polished 1980s-esque Peralta S. For the follow-up, Giugiaro wanted to draw a deeper connection to the owner. As an industrialist, Peralta has business interests involving copper, so Giugiaro suggested it as the material.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Giugiaro’s name is well known in the automotive world. His father, Giorgetto Giugiaro, is a master of clean-line designs—he penned the DeLorean DMC-12, the BMW M1, the original Lotus Esprit, and the first Volkswagen Golf. The senior Giugiaro’s career has included work for Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, and many more of the world’s most notable automotive brands. The father-and-son duo founded GFG Style together over a decade ago, but it’s only been in recent years that they’ve been dedicating their talents to bespoke coachbuilt cars for individual collectors, as with the Peralta D.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

In a recent development, and while using copper for a car’s bodywork may be unorthodox, the designer claims it wasn’t as difficult as it may seem. “It really surprised us that copper proved to be much more malleable than the aluminum we had worked with previously; it is also considerably easier to weld and polish,” Fabrizio says. “Of course, it does come with the disadvantage of greater weight, but since it was combined with a supporting structure made entirely of carbon fiber, the overall balance between the materials ultimately worked out well.”.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Recent findings suggest that beneath all that copper lies the chassis of a 2025 Maserati GranTurismo Trofeo—itself a stylish design, but one far removed from the almost brutalist simplicity of the Peralta D’s angles. Instead of traditional doors, the car features a dramatic opening system inspired by the Peralta S’s single-motion dome, with independently opening side windows and gullwing-style openings at the rear to access the back seats.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

In a recent development, inside, copper-colored leather adorns most surfaces, broken up (almost) only by the infotainment and dashboard screens, which offer some of the few hints of its Maserati roots. Meant to showcase the bond between its owner and his daughters, the car comes with a few (perhaps stereotypically) female-oriented features, such as a passenger-side makeup station with an illuminated mirror and dedicated cosmetic storage. And while the rear seats are tight, a retractable refrigerator designed to hold a bottle of champagne and four copper glasses means occupants can easily distract themselves.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

While the Peralta D might seem to push the boundaries—or at least the materials—of road-going automobile design to their limits, Fabrizio suggests even wilder builds may follow in its tire tracks.

“I have another alternative material in mind, one that has only ever been used once before,” he says, “so it will be another surprise…”.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Will Sabel Courtney has been working in journalism since 2010, specializing primarily in automotive and men’s lifestyle writing. He has driven too many cars to count over the course of his career. A native of Vermont, he has lived in Newly introduced York City for two decades, dividing his time between Manhattan and Brooklyn, where he now resides.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hybrid and remote work have changed what people expect from a modern workspace. No longer do people want fixed seating or single-purpose design. Instead, they are looking for modular, multi-use furniture that boosts productivity while maintaining comfort and style. When Chris and Jon Panichella set out to design their latest seating collection for Arcadia, they turned to everyday life for inspiration.

“The idea for Almeya began with a woman working from an inflatable raft at the beach,” the Panichellas explain. “She could recline and read in one position, then sit up and work in another—a simple moment that captured how much people now expect from their spaces: comfort, flexibility, and function. That observation became the very first concept sketch that eventually evolved into the Almeya offering we know today.”.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

With a full family of products—including modular, lounge, work-lounge, benches, and occasional tables—the Almeya Collection offers a fluid experience that adapts to these modern shifts in productivity and collaboration. Across the series, soft, organic forms invite comfort and ease, while integrated tables, flexible configurations, and strategic power stations allow for both focus and sociability.

According to recent reports, almeya began with a single lounge chair and an integrated two-tiered side table. The idea was simple: the combination could function as a self-contained work island, with two separate surfaces, power access, and an optional rotating tablet. With this concept in mind, the Panichellas developed a standalone lounge chair, love seat, and sofa with the same flexible spirit. (Case in point: The swivel-base lounge chair allows for adaptability and easy collaboration). Finally, the complete collection came together, designed to support the various—and often unpredictable—ways people work and gather.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

Recent findings suggest that to inspire interaction, designers are encouraged to group lounge seating intermittently to foster spontaneous connections. To create pathways or natural flow within a space, they can explore Almeya’s modular capabilities. The organic curves of the lounge models also create an inviting warmth, blurring the line between contract and residential. And for healthcare and education settings, optional clean-outs are offered between the seat and back.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

Completing the collection, occasional tables carry the same gentle, organic language for a cohesive experience. Available in multiple sizes and shapes, tables feature upholstered sides and are offered with ash or walnut veneer, laminate, Corian, and Fenix top surfaces.

See the full Almeya Series at arcadiacontract.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

According to recent reports, yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

In a recent development, unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

In fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

Sources indicate that one of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

To ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

Because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

Industry observers note that an audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Sources indicate that finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

Industry observers note that the more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

Latest Update: As Route 66 shifts into its centennial year, preservation efforts accelerate

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • US Route 66 officially started on 11 November 1926 with the launch of the nation’s first federal highway system.
  • Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, with the new highways bypassing its Art Deco service stations and mid-century diners.
  • Industry observers note that “We want to let people outside of Route 66 know that it’s more than what you think it is,” indicates Rhys Martin, manager of the Preserve Route 66 Initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US Route 66 officially started on 11 November 1926 with the launch of the nation’s first federal highway system. With the spread of affordable automobiles after the Second World War, it became a destination. A unique vernacular culture formed along its almost 2,500 miles running through eight states from Chicago, Illinois to Santa Monica, California, from neon signs enticing travellers to themed motels to roadside attractions with concrete and fibreglass sculptures.

Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, with the new highways bypassing its Art Deco service stations and mid-century diners. Now, 100 years after its debut, there are efforts across the country to preserve what survives from what was once the “Main Street of America”.

Industry observers note that “We want to let people outside of Route 66 know that it’s more than what you think it is,” indicates Rhys Martin, manager of the Preserve Route 66 Initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “Most people think of ’57 Chevys and cheeseburgers and Marilyn Monroe, and there’s a lot of that, but there’s so much more. It ties together so many diverse cultures, from Native American to African American. In my home state of Oklahoma, it goes through the Asian District [in Oklahoma City], which sprung up around Vietnamese refugees during the war. In West Hollywood, Route 66 has a huge LGBTQ presence.”.

Grants from the Preserve Route 66 Initiative reflect that range of history, which is often overlooked in the nostalgia for its Americana. There are structural repair needs, like at the Fanning 66 Outpost in Cuba, Missouri, which hosts a 42ft-high rocking chair (the world’s largest until 2015), as well as storytelling projects, such as mapping Native American experiences along the corridor, as it passes through many tribal and ancestral lands yet has had little representation of their voices. Care for the road extends to the scarce sections of its original pavement. Through local advocacy, what is known as the Ribbon Road in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, which has the last segment of a 9ft-wide design made for Model Ts, was partially protected from resurfacing this year.

Sources indicate that “You might think a pavement’s not art, but when you get out and look at it, especially compared to what it is today, it is very different,” Martin says. “I have come to really appreciate it from a craftsmanship perspective, but also a longevity perspective. These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life, and the fact that I get to drive these same roads tells a story.”.

Sources indicate that advocacy is under way to give National Historic Trail designation to Route 66, with a bipartisan bill introduced last year. Martin notes that Route 66 is now similar to how it was before 1926, when it was a loose network of roads, and this legislation would help bring together its fragmented parts.

It has been revealed that “It gets people to sit at the same table, like the state Route 66 associations, the National Park Service and the Department of Transportation, so that we can find ways to work together for corridor-wide initiatives and to help elevate preservation needs,” he says. “The corridor continues to evolve, and buildings are threatened all the time with demolition or augmentation beyond recognition, and being designated as a National Historic Trail is not a roadblock. But it is something to say, this is notable and we need to take care when the fabric of the road might be forever altered.”.

Coca Cola painting on a brick wall, along Route 66 in Stroud, Oklahoma Courtesy National Trust for Historic Preservation.

Recent findings suggest that local groups, municipalities and individuals are stewarding Route 66’s relics. Martin is also the president of the Oklahoma Route 66 Association, which is restoring a U-Haul painted by the late artist Bob Waldmire, who illustrated maps and postcards of the road’s built and natural wonders. The city of Catoosa in Oklahoma acquired the beloved roadside Blue Whale in 2020 from the family of Hugh S. Davis, who in 1972 sculpted the 80ft-long attraction from concrete as a gift for his wife. Last May, a latest Blue Whale Visitor Center opened with retro illuminated signage.

The city of Albuquerque opened a Route 66 Visitor Center last April and its park features a collection of restored roadside signs. Among them is the first major project from the Friends of the Orphan Signs (FOS), an organisation that since 2010 has worked on revitalising abandoned signs, particularly in Albuquerque’s underserved neighbourhoods.

Lindsey Fromm, the executive director of FOS, states that many of these signs are for places that were razed during the city’s removal of derelict buildings: “There were areas of Route 66 with dozens of towering empty signs.”.

Sources indicate that most Route 66 sign restorations return them to their former glory; FOS reimagines them as public art. Revivir (2012) at the fresh visitor centre was created with students who designed visuals responding to local nature that were bordered with purple neon.

“While artists lead these sign projects, they will collaborate with communities, archives, the surrounding environment, or will collect histories and stories to create the work that is displayed, so that it speaks to the immediate moment and surrounding community who live, work and travel by the sign,” Fromm states.

According to recent reports, projects like this are not just about preserving places for tourists but Route 66’s role in daily life. These grassroots and national efforts recognise that even though it is no longer a main thoroughfare, it is still a vital place of connection from the Midwest to the Pacific, for communities both urban and rural, and between the visitors and residents brought together on their journeys.
